central_claim: An open-weight LLM run inside the hospital network extracts valvular heart disease severity from echocardiography reports more accurately than rule-based extraction and keeps its accuracy at a second centre, with the remaining errors concentrated in reports that grade a lesion between two categories.

alternatives.text: An open-weight LLM extracts valvular heart disease severity more accurately than a rule-based system at two centres.
alternatives.why_not: Conservative. True but reads as better numbers only, and drops the error finding that tells registries what to fix.

alternatives.text: Locally deployed open-weight LLMs can replace manual abstraction for valvular heart disease registries.
alternatives.why_not: Bold. The study measured report-level accuracy retrospectively, not registry completeness or staff time, so the design cannot carry it.

gap: Whether an open-weight LLM run inside the hospital can extract valvular heart disease severity accurately, and keep that accuracy at a centre not used for development, is not known.
aim: To compare an open-weight LLM run on hospital hardware with a rule-based system for extracting valvular heart disease severity from echocardiography reports at two Swiss centres, against cardiologist labels.
design: Retrospective two-centre study of 1,200 consecutive transthoracic echocardiography reports (2022 to 2023). Prompts were developed on 200 reports from centre A and tested on 1,000 reports from both centres. Two cardiologists with consensus adjudication formed the reference standard. A 70-billion-parameter open-weight model was used without fine-tuning, with bootstrap 95% CIs.

results.statement: The two cardiologists agreed on 94.1% of lesion grades before consensus (kappa 0.89, 95% CI 0.86 to 0.92).
results.source: results.md, Study population and reference standard

results.statement: The LLM achieved an accuracy of 96.3% (95% CI 95.1 to 97.4) compared with 88.7% (87.0 to 90.4) for the rule-based system.
The difference in accuracy was 7.6 percentage points (95% CI 5.8 to 9.4).
At centre B, not used for prompt development, the LLM reached an accuracy of 95.8% (95% CI 93.9 to 97.5).
Mean processing time was 4.1 s per report.
Of 37 LLM errors, 24 (64.9%) occurred in reports that graded a lesion between two categories.

implications.statement: An open-weight model run inside the hospital is an alternative to rule-based extraction where reports cannot leave the network.
Accuracy may transfer between hospitals with similar reporting habits without new prompt development.
Allowing an intermediate grade, or standardising report templates, may reduce errors more than further prompt tuning.
Prospective validation within a registry workflow should precede routine use.
